# Substance-related and addictive disorders

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Neurology > Toxic and metabolic disorders > Substance-related and addictive disorders*

[Original Article Link](/library/oP00fT)

---

## Summary

Substance-related and addictive disorders are a category of conditions in the <u>DSM-5</u> that include <u>substance-use disorders</u> (<u>SUDs</u>), <u>substance-induced disorders</u>, and <u>gambling disorder</u> (a non-substance-related addictive disorder). These disorders are characterized by often increasingly risky use of addictive substances and/or engagement in harmful behaviors despite significant <u>distress</u> and/or adverse consequences. Substance use can lead to physical and psychological dependence, including <u>substance tolerance</u> and withdrawal with dose reduction or cessation. Substance-related and addictive disorders are associated with criminal behavior, social isolation, housing instability, declining academic or professional performance, and new or worsening psychiatric comorbidities (e.g., <u>major depressive disorder</u>, <u>psychosis</u>, <u>anxiety disorder</u>). Treatment typically involves counseling (e.g., <u>motivational interviewing</u>), <u>psychotherapy</u> (e.g., <u>cognitive-behavioral therapy</u>), and/or pharmacotherapy.

---

## Classification

* <u>Substance use disorders</u>: a class of psychiatric disorders characterized by a pattern of continued use of an addictive substance despite significant substance-use-related impairment or <u>distress</u>

* <u>Substance-induced disorders</u>

* Substance intoxication

* <u>Substance withdrawal</u>

* Substance/medication-induced mental disorders: a class of disorders comprising the effects of intoxication or withdrawal and psychiatric disorders secondary to the use of a substance, including prescription medication

* Non-substance-related addictive disorders: a class of psychiatric disorders characterized by excessive behavioral patterns producing symptoms comparable to those seen in <u>SUDs</u>  [[1]](/library/muWV7M0)

---

## Definitions

### Substance use disorder [[2]](/library/Nta-dm)[[3]](/library/p-aLyM)[[4]](/library/J-asyM)




* Description: a chronic condition in which an uncontrolled pattern of substance use leads to significant physical, psychological, and social impairment or <u>distress</u>, with continued use despite substance-related problems.

* <u>Epidemiology</u>

* Sex: <u>♂</u> > <u>♀</u>

* <u>Alcohol</u> and <u>nicotine</u> use are most common.

* Characteristics: features that are typical for all <u>substance use disorders</u> (≥ 2 features must occur within 1 year to fulfill the <u>DSM-V</u> criteria) 

* Impaired control

* Using a substance in larger amounts and/or for a longer time than originally intended

* Repeated failed attempts to cut down on use

* A great deal of time spent on substance-related activities (e.g., seeking out, buying, using, recovering from use)

* Intense desire to obtain and use substance (craving)

* Social impairment

* Problems fulfilling work, school, family, or social obligations (e.g., not attending work or school, neglecting children or partner)

* Problems with interpersonal relationships directly related to substance use (withdrawal from relationships, marital issues)

* Reduced social, occupational, and recreational activities (e.g., less time socializing with friends, neglecting hobbies)

* Risky use

* Use in physically hazardous situations;  (e.g., driving a car under the influence, unprotected sex, operating heavy machinery)

* Continued use despite awareness of problems related to or exacerbated by substance use (e.g., continued <u>alcohol</u> use despite having <u>cirrhosis</u>)

* Pharmacologic indicators 

* Drug tolerance: the need to continuously increase the dose of a substance to achieve the same desired effect

* Drug withdrawal: a substance-dependent collection of symptoms that appear after cessation of prolonged heavy drug use accompanied by a strong urge to readminister the substance

* Often, <u>withdrawal symptoms</u> are the opposite of intoxication effects, e.g., <u>heroin intoxication</u> causes sedation and <u>constipation</u>, whereas <u>heroin withdrawal</u> causes <u>anxiety</u>, <u>insomnia</u>, and <u>diarrhea</u>.

* Hallucinogens and inhalants do not cause withdrawal.

* Exception: patients undergoing supervised treatment with certain psychoactive substances (e.g., stimulants, <u>cocaine</u>, <u>opioids</u>, <u>nitrous oxide</u>, <u>sedative-hypnotic drugs</u>, <u>anxiolytic drugs</u>, <u>cannabis</u>) [[5]](/library/MEcMwV0)

* Tolerance and withdrawal can be normal physiological adaptations.

* In the absence of other <u>DSM-V</u> criteria, tolerance and withdrawal do not necessarily indicate <u>substance use disorder</u>.





> [!WARNING]
> Withdrawal from some substances, such as <u>alcohol</u>, <u>benzodiazepines</u>, and <u>barbiturates</u>, can be fatal!




### Substance-induced disorders




* Intoxication: a temporary condition caused by recent ingestion of a substance that alters a person's consciousness, <u>cognition</u>, perception, judgment, affect, and/or behavior; commonly occurs in <u>substance use disorders</u> but also in one-off use

* Withdrawal: a condition characterized by behavioral, physiological, and cognitive changes caused by a sudden reduction or cessation of substance intake after a prolonged period of heavy intake; usually occurs in association with <u>substance use disorders</u>

* Substance/medication-induced mental disorders: a psychiatric disorder that develops within 1 month of intoxication or withdrawal of a substance and is not attributable to an independent mental disorder (e.g., <u>substance/medication-induced anxiety disorder</u>)





### Related definitions




* Abuse

* In the context of substance use, the term “abuse” should generally be avoided due to its impreciseness  and the historical burden of stigma.

* “Substance use” is generally the preferred term in this context, with “substance misuse” being appropriate in the context of prescription drugs.

* Drug-seeking behavior

* A maladaptive behavioral response to substance addiction that involves manipulative and/or demanding behaviors to obtain the desired substance

* Often indicative of an underlying <u>substance use disorder</u>

* Examples of <u>drug-seeking behavior</u>

* Faking/aggravating symptoms

* Bribes, threats, theft (e.g., prescription pads)

* Forging prescriptions or using those of others (e.g., under the names of family members)

* Pretending to lose prescriptions and asking for new ones

* Insisting that a treatment that does not involve one or more certain (addictive) drugs is ineffective or not tolerated (e.g., due to an alleged <u>allergy</u>)

* Demanding a stronger medication or higher dose due to an allegedly high <u>drug tolerance</u>

* Claiming that another, an ostensibly more experienced or more caring, physician would prescribe the desired drug or threatening to see another physician if the desired drug is not prescribed.

* Medication-assisted treatment (<u>MAT</u>): treatment for <u>substance use disorder</u> that combines counseling with pharmacological and <u>behavioral therapy</u>, tailored to each patient's needs.  [[6]](/library/l01vT20)

## Management of substance use disorder

### SUD screening [[9]](/library/P01WT20)




#### Indications




* Tobacco use: all adults and pregnant individuals [[10]](/library/KvcUae0)

* <u>Unhealthy alcohol use</u>: adults in primary care settings [[11]](/library/BwczOe0)

* <u>Unhealthy drug use</u>: adults, if treatment can be offered  [[12]](/library/g-cF9U0)





#### Validated screening tools




* <u>Alcohol use disorders identification test-concise</u> (<u>AUDIT-C</u>)  [[11]](/library/BwczOe0)

* <u>Single alcohol screening question</u> (<u>SASQ</u>) [[11]](/library/BwczOe0)

* Tobacco, <u>alcohol</u>, prescription medication, and other substance use tool (TAPS) [[12]](/library/g-cF9U0)

* <u>National Institute on Drug Abuse (NIDA) quick screen</u> [[12]](/library/g-cF9U0)





> [!WARNING]
> The harms of screening for <u>unhealthy drug use</u> outweigh the benefits when treatment cannot be provided or when findings may result in punitive actions (e.g., some US state laws penalize pregnant individuals who use substances or seek addiction treatment). [[12]](/library/g-cF9U0)




![Alcohol Use Disorders Identification Test-Concise (AUDIT-C)](media/rzwgxqne1xy4qpmdivr1k9s5.jpg)

Alcohol Use Disorders Identification Test-Concise (AUDIT-C)




### SUD assessment [[6]](/library/l01vT20)




* Indications

* Positive <u>SUD screening</u>

* History of <u>SUD</u>

* <u>Classic toxidrome</u> or findings that suggest <u>drug intoxication or withdrawal</u>, e.g.:

* <u>Altered mental status</u>, acute <u>agitation</u>

* Acute cardiopulmonary symptoms

* Needle or track marks

* Prior to initiating a long-term <u>opioid</u> or <u>benzodiazepine</u> prescription

* Components

* Cravings and <u>withdrawal symptoms</u>

* Reasons, amount, frequency, route, and duration of substance use

* Impact on overall well-being

* Prior experiences with treatment, including:

* Facilitators (e.g., coping skills, recovery supports)

* Barriers (e.g., triggers, mobility impairment, <u>health literacy</u>)

* Current level of interest in treatment

* Further evaluation

* Screen all patients for coexisting disorders (e.g., <u>intimate partner violence</u>, <u>mood disorders</u>, <u>anxiety</u>).

* Consider <u>drug testing</u> if results will impact management.





> [!TIP]
> The <u>screening, brief intervention, and referral to treatment</u> (<u>SBIRT</u>) model may be used to identify and assess <u>SUD</u> in any care setting. [[6]](/library/l01vT20)




### Drug testing [[13]](/library/N01-T20)[[14]](/library/m01Vg20)



* Definition: the testing of biological samples for the presence of drugs and drug metabolites




#### Urine drug test




* Overview

* Immunoassay testing is the most frequently used method for <u>urine drug testing</u>.

* <u>Mass spectrometry</u>/gas chromatography is used to confirm immunoassay results.

* Example situations for the use of a <u>urine drug test</u> include workup of <u>altered mental status</u> and monitoring during <u>SUD</u> treatment or <u>chronic opioid therapy</u>.

* Detectable substances (immunoassay)

* <u>Phencyclidine</u> (<u>PCP</u>)

* <u>Opioids</u>

* <u>THC</u> (<u>marijuana</u>)

* <u>Cocaine</u>

* <u>Amphetamine</u>

* Undetectable substances (immunoassay)

* <u>GHB</u>

* <u>MDMA</u>

* Semisynthetic and synthetic <u>opioids</u>

* <u>Ketamine</u>

* <u>Psilocybin</u> (hallucinogenic mushrooms), DMT (ayahuasca), <u>mescaline</u> (peyote)

* Synthetic drugs

* Substances that can cause cross-reactivity and yield <u>false positive</u> results [[15]](/library/K3XUjB)

* <u>Marijuana</u>: food containing hemp

* <u>PCP</u>: <u>doxylamine</u>, <u>dextromethorphan</u>, <u>tramadol</u>

* <u>Opioids</u>: poppy seeds, <u>rifampin</u>

* <u>Benzodiazepines</u>: <u>sertraline</u>

* <u>Amphetamines</u>: <u>pseudoephedrine</u>, <u>ephedrine</u>, <u>phenylephrine</u>, <u>metformin</u>





> [!WARNING]
> <u>Urine drug test</u> immunoassays can generate <u>false-positive</u> and <u>false-negative</u> results because of cross-reactivity with other medications (e.g., <u>rifampin</u> with <u>opioid</u> assays, <u>sertraline</u> with <u>benzodiazepines</u>, <u>metformin</u> with <u>amphetamines</u>). [[13]](/library/N01-T20)




#### Blood/serum <u>drug test</u>




* Usage: assess intoxication or impairment in emergency situations

* Examples: <u>drug overdosage</u>, after <u>motor vehicle crash</u>





#### <u>Laboratory methods</u>




* Immunoassays

* Rapid presumptive results for many substances (e.g., point-of-care <u>urine drug tests</u>)

* Provide quantitative results

* Can generate <u>false-positive</u> and/or <u>false-negative</u> results

* <u>Mass spectrometry</u>

* Often obtained based on a presumptive positive result

* Definitive results

* Can provide quantitative drug levels





> [!TIP]
> Always confirm qualitative point-of-care <u>drug test</u> results (i.e., with <u>mass spectrometry</u>) when the results might have legal, financial, or employment implications.




### Management




* Treatment options depend on the respective substance being used (e.g., “<u>Management of alcohol withdrawal</u>” and “<u>Opioid withdrawal</u>”) and patient preferences.

* Utilize <u>person-centered language</u>, <u>motivational interviewing</u>, and strategies for <u>harm reduction in OUD</u>. [[16]](/library/4013T20)

* Manage withdrawal, if present.

* Medication-assisted treatment (<u>MAT</u>): treatment for <u>substance use disorder</u> that combines counseling with pharmacological and <u>behavioral therapy</u>, tailored to each patient's needs.  [[6]](/library/l01vT20)





#### Disposition [[17]](/library/Nsc-Ed0)[[18]](/library/kscmEd0)




The most appropriate treatment setting may change over time and is influenced by: [[19]](/library/Xsc9td0)




* The presence and severity of <u>withdrawal symptoms</u> and/or comorbid conditions

* Patient preference and <u>social history</u>

* Current circumstances

* Social support

* Need for medication oversight (e.g., <u>methadone</u>)

| <br>Hospital withdrawal management | <br><br>* Significant comorbidities, e.g.:<br><br>* <u>Sepsis</u><br><br>* Co-ingestions<br><br>* <u>Suicidality</u><br><br>* <u>Heart failure</u><br><br>* Need for 24-hour respiratory and/or <u>hemodynamic monitoring</u>, e.g.:<br><br>* Severe <u>withdrawal symptoms</u><br><br>* Clinically unstable<br><br>* High medication dosages<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Inpatient treatment program<br><br>* Daily physician evaluations<br><br>* Addiction services<br><br><br> |
| Residential | <br><br>* Severe withdrawal<br><br>* Need for 24-hour support<br><br>* Outpatient withdrawal treatment is neither safe nor feasible.<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Inpatient treatment program<br><br>* Access to a physician<br><br>* Addiction services<br><br><br> |
| Intensive outpatient | <br>* Patients with:<br><br>* Need for daily support<br><br>* Reliable means to access care (e.g., transportation)<br><br>* A supportive living environment<br><br> | <br><br>* Outpatient programs in specialized centers<br><br>* High patient oversight<br><br>* Direct administration of medications (e.g., <u>methadone</u>)<br><br><br> |
| Outpatient | <br>* Stable patients with:<br><br>* Less than daily support needs<br><br>* A secure living environment<br><br>* High general functioning<br><br> | <br><br>* Home or clinic setting<br><br>* Lower patient oversight than intensive <u>outpatient WM</u><br><br>* Physicians prescribe medications for outpatient use.<br><br><br> |





> [!WARNING]
> Forced treatment is not recommended as it is often followed by relapse and a loss of trust in treatment services and providers.

---

## Alcohol-related disorders

See the article “<u>Overview of alcohol use</u>,” “<u>Alcohol intoxication</u>,” “<u>Alcohol use disorder</u>,” and “<u>Alcohol withdrawal</u>.”

---

## Caffeine-related disorders

* Substance: caffeine (usually ingested with coffee, tea, soda, or energy drinks) [[7]](/library/qLbCA8)[[20]](/library/ILbY_8)

* Mechanism of action: <u>adenosine</u> <u>antagonist</u> → increased <u>cAMP</u> → neurological excitation and facilitated <u>catecholamine</u> release [[20]](/library/ILbY_8)

* <u>Epidemiology</u>:

* <u>Caffeine</u> is the most widely consumed psychoactive substance in the world. [[21]](/library/BLbz-8)

* ∼ 7% of the US population expericence symptoms consistent with <u>caffeine</u> intoxication. [[2]](/library/Nta-dm)

* Clinical features of intoxication

* To meet the <u>DSM-V</u> criteria for <u>caffeine</u> intoxication, individuals must exhibit at least five of the following symptoms shortly after <u>caffeine</u> intake. [[2]](/library/Nta-dm)

* <u>Psychomotor agitation</u>

* Excitement

* <u>Insomnia</u>

* Incoherent speech and/or chaotic flow of thoughts

* Muscle twitching

* Flushed face

* <u>Cardiac arrhythmias</u> or <u>tachycardia</u>

* Severe restlessness

* <u>Anxiety</u>, nervousness

* Inexhaustibility

* Diuresis

* Gastrointestinal disturbance

* The following features may be also present: [[2]](/library/Nta-dm)[[20]](/library/ILbY_8)[[21]](/library/BLbz-8)

* <u>Tremor</u>

* <u>Light flashes</u>

* <u>Tinnitus</u>

* <u>Seizures</u>

* <u>Headache</u>

* Doses of about 10 g of <u>caffeine</u> can be lethal. [[20]](/library/ILbY_8)

* Clinical features of withdrawal: The <u>DSM-V</u> requires at least three of the following symptoms to be present within 24 hours after abrupt reduction of <u>caffeine</u> intake to account for <u>caffeine</u> withdrawal [[2]](/library/Nta-dm)

* Caffeine withdrawal headache

* <u>Depressed mood</u>, irritability

* Drowsiness, fatigue

* Difficulty concentrating

* <u>Flu-like symptoms</u>, muscle <u>pain</u>

* Related disorders

* <u>Caffeine</u>-induced <u>anxiety disorder</u> (see “<u>Anxiety disorders</u>”)

* <u>Caffeine</u>-induced <u>sleep disorders</u> (see “<u>Delayed sleep phase disorder</u>”)

* Treatment [[22]](/library/iZYJYn)[[23]](/library/QZYuYn)

* Overdose: supportive therapy (e.g., <u>beta-blockers</u> for <u>tachyarrhythmia</u>)

* Withdrawal: Symptoms typically manifest within 24 hours after the last intake and resolve spontaneously within 10 days.

---

## Cannabis-related disorders

* Cannabis use disorder: <u>DSM-V</u> requires ≥ 2 of the following features to occur within a 1-year period of <u>cannabis</u> use, accompanied by <u>agitation</u> and severe impairment of functioning 

* Using <u>cannabis</u> in larger amounts or over a longer period than intended

* Persistent desire to cut down the amount of <u>cannabis</u> used or repeated unsuccessful efforts to stop using it

* A large amount of time is spent using <u>cannabis</u>, trying to acquire it, or recovering from its effects

* Strong craving to consume <u>cannabis</u>

* <u>Cannabis</u> use has a negative impact on social and professional function (e.g., at work, school, or home)

* Continued <u>cannabis</u> use despite social or interpersonal problems that are directly caused or exacerbated by its use

* Loss of interest in activities that were important to user prior to regular <u>cannabis</u> use

* Recurrent use of <u>cannabis</u> in situations in which its use is associated with the risk of physical harm (e.g., driving a car)

* Continued <u>cannabis</u> use despite persistent or recurrent psychological or physical problems that can most likely be attributed directly to the use of <u>cannabis</u>

* Tolerance, which can manifest as:

* The need to markedly increase the amount of <u>cannabis</u> to achieve the desired effect/intoxication
and/or

* A reduced effect over time when the same amount of <u>cannabis</u> is used

* Withdrawal, which can manifest in the form of:

* Clinical features of <u>cannabis withdrawal</u>
and/or

* Substance use to alleviate or avoid <u>withdrawal symptoms</u>

* Other <u>cannabis-induced disorders</u> 

* <u>Cannabis intoxication</u>

* <u>Cannabis withdrawal</u>

* <u>Cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome</u>

* <u>Cannabis-related psychiatric disorders</u>

* Medical disorders, e.g., pulmonary problems or reduced <u>fertility</u>

* See “<u>Cannabis-induced disorders</u>” for details.

---

## Hallucinogen-related disorders

Hallucinogens are a heterogeneous group of substances that can trigger <u>hallucinations</u> following exposure. These substances have varying mechanisms of action and associated physiological and neuropsychiatric effects.




### Substances with hallucinogenic properties [[24]](/library/dJWoGm0)[[25]](/library/VJWGGm0)




Commonly used substances include:




* Classic hallucinogens (psychedelics)

* <u>Lysergic acid diethylamide</u> (<u>LSD</u>)

* <u>Psilocybin</u>

* Dimethyltryptamine (DMT)

* Dissociative drugs

* <u>Phencyclidine</u> (<u>PCP</u>)

* <u>Ketamine</u>

* <u>Dextromethorphan</u> (at high doses)  [[26]](/library/eJWxGm0)

* Serotonergic stimulants

* <u>MDMA</u>

* <u>Mescaline</u>

* Botanicals

* Ayahuasca

* <u>Cannabis</u>

* Salvia divinorum





> [!WARNING]
> <u>LSD</u>, DMT, <u>psilocybin</u>, and <u>MDMA</u> are controlled substances in the United States. [[24]](/library/dJWoGm0)




> [!TIP]
> Classic hallucinogens may be beneficial for the <u>treatment of depression</u> and <u>anxiety</u>. [[27]](/library/fJWktm0)




### Hallucinogen intoxication




* Clinical features: The <u>DSM-V</u> requires the following features to be present during or shortly after the use of hallucinogens (other than <u>phencyclidine</u>) for the diagnosis of intoxication. [[2]](/library/Nta-dm)

* Behavioral/mental (<u>paranoid</u> ideation, <u>anxiety</u>, <u>depression</u>, fear of “going crazy”, impaired judgment)

* Perceptual (<u>synesthesia</u>, <u>derealization</u>, <u>depersonalization</u>, <u>illusions</u>)

* At least 2 of the following somatic symptoms:

* <u>Tachycardia</u>

* <u>Palpitations</u>

* <u>Mydriasis</u>

* <u>Diaphoresis</u>

* <u>Tremor</u>

* Incoordination

* Blurred <u>vision</u>

* Treatment [[7]](/library/qLbCA8)

* Most hallucinogen intoxications are treated with <u>supportive care</u>, e.g.:

* <u>Antipsychotics</u> for <u>substance-induced psychosis</u>

* <u>Benzodiazepines for agitation</u>

* External cooling for <u>hyperthermia</u>

* Some substances require specific management.

* See “<u>PCP</u>.”

* See “<u>MDMA</u>.”

* See “<u>Cannabis intoxication</u>.”





### Hallucinogen withdrawal




* Hallucinogens are not typically associated with symptoms of withdrawal.

* <u>Withdrawal symptoms</u> (e.g., cravings) may occur in chronic <u>MDMA</u> users; see “Stimulant withdrawal.” [[28]](/library/cmWaeN0)





### Hallucinogen persisting perception disorder (<u>HPPD</u>; flashbacks) [[29]](/library/0KbeUu)




* Episodic or continuous symptoms (optical <u>hallucinations</u>, <u>depression</u>, and panic) that occur weeks after the initial intoxication

* Spontaneous recurrence of acute <u>hallucinogen intoxication</u> due to reabsorption of the intoxicating substance from bodily stores

---

## Phencyclidine use disorder

* Substance: phencyclidine (<u>PCP</u>); the liquid form is often sprayed on tobacco or <u>cannabis</u> and smoked.

* Street names: <u>angel dust</u>, peace pill, elephant tranquilizer, hog [[30]](/library/h5YcPp)

* Mechanism of action [[30]](/library/h5YcPp)

* Inhibits <u>dopamine</u>, <u>serotonin</u>, and <u>norepinephrine</u> reuptake

* Antagonizes <u>NMDA receptors</u> → stimulant or depressive neurological effects (dose dependent)

* Binds to the <u>sigma receptor</u> complex

* Clinical features

* <u>Phencyclidine use disorder</u>

* Signs of injury, e.g., due to fights, accidents

* <u>Memory</u> and speech deficits

* Cognitive impairment

* <u>PCP</u> intoxication: The <u>DSM-V</u> requires the following features to be present to account for <u>phencyclidine</u> (or pharmacologically similar substance) intoxication [[2]](/library/Nta-dm)[[31]](/library/35YSPp)

* Behavioral changes (violence, belligerence, <u>psychomotor agitation</u>, impulsiveness, impaired judgment) must develop during or shortly after the use of <u>phencyclidine</u> or similar substance

* At least 2 of the following signs should be present within an hour after the use of <u>phencyclidine</u> or similar substance

* <u>Hypertension</u>, <u>tachycardia</u>, <u>dysrhythmias</u>

* Horizontal or vertical <u>nystagmus</u>

* <u>Ataxia</u>

* <u>Dysarthria</u>

* Muscle rigidity

* <u>Hyperacusis</u>

* <u>Seizures</u> or <u>coma</u>

* Decreased sensation to pinprick (increased <u>pain</u> tolerance)

* The following features may be also present [[2]](/library/Nta-dm)[[32]](/library/gobFYu)

* <u>Miosis</u>

* <u>Hyperthermia</u>

* <u>Synesthesia</u>

* Confusion, <u>disorientation</u>

* <u>Delirium</u>

* <u>Amnesia</u>

* <u>Phencyclidine</u>-induced mental disorders: <u>psychosis</u>;  (e.g., <u>hallucinations</u>), <u>mania</u>

* Treatment of <u>PCP</u> intoxication [[30]](/library/h5YcPp)[[31]](/library/35YSPp)

* Reduction of environmental stimuli

* <u>Gastrointestinal decontamination</u>

* <u>Supportive care</u>

* Sedation with <u>benzodiazepines</u> (for severe <u>agitation</u>) or <u>haloperidol</u> (if psychotic symptoms are present)

* Complications

* Trauma (commonly accompanied by <u>intracranial hemorrhage</u>)

* <u>Seizures</u>

* <u>Rhabdomyolysis</u>

* Reabsorption of the drug in the <u>gastrointestinal tract</u> may lead recurrence of symptoms.

---

## Other hallucinogen use disorder

### LSD [[7]](/library/qLbCA8)




* Substance: <u>lysergic acid diethylamide</u>

* Street names: acid

* Mechanism of action: 5HT<sub>2A</sub>-<u>serotonin</u>-<u>receptor</u> <u>agonist</u> (increased <u>serotonin</u> concentrations in the <u>synaptic cleft</u> → <u>hallucinations</u>)

* Specific clinical features of intoxication

* Mental changes: marked <u>anxiety</u> and <u>paranoia</u>, <u>psychosis</u>

* Perceptual changes: <u>Depersonalization</u>, visual and/or auditory perceptual distortion, and <u>synesthesia</u> are particularly noticeable.

* Flashbacks (rarely unsettling)

* <u>Mydriasis</u>

* Treatment of intoxication

* <u>Supportive care</u>, reassurance

* <u>Psychotic symptoms</u>: <u>first-generation antipsychotics</u>

* <u>Anxiety</u>: <u>benzodiazepines</u>

* <u>Hallucinogen use disorder</u>: <u>Substance use disorders</u> due to <u>LSD</u> are rare. [[33]](/library/TJW6tm0)





### Phenethylamine derivatives




A class of substances with serotonergic and <u>sympathomimetic</u> effects




* <u>MDMA</u>

* Intoxication is associated with <u>serotonin syndrome</u> and <u>hyponatremia</u>; see “<u>Stimulant intoxication</u>” for details. [[34]](/library/1Kb22u)

* <u>Substance use disorders</u> related to <u>MDMA</u> are poorly defined. [[28]](/library/cmWaeN0)

* Misuse and dependence can occur, but are less likely and usually less severe than other stimulants.

* Standard <u>management of substance use disorders</u> is recommended.  [[28]](/library/cmWaeN0)

* Mescaline

* A hallucinogen found in the peyote cactus

* Street names: mesc, cactus, buttons

* Management of intoxication is similar to that of <u>MDMA</u> (see “<u>Stimulant intoxication</u>” and “<u>Serotonin syndrome</u>”).

* <u>Mescaline</u> is rarely involved in <u>substance use disorders</u>. [[35]](/library/UJWbtm0)[[36]](/library/gJWFtm0)

---

## Inhalant-related disorders

* Substances: hydrocarbon-based inhalants (e.g., glue, paint thinners, fuel, <u>nitrous oxide</u>, alkyl nitrites) [[2]](/library/Nta-dm)[[37]](/library/gZYFan)

* Street names: poppers (alkyl nitrite); <u>whippits</u> (<u>nitrous oxide</u>)

* <u>Epidemiology</u>: most prevalent in high-school-aged individuals [[37]](/library/gZYFan)

* Mechanism of action: : Inhalants generally work by depressing the <u>CNS</u>. [[37]](/library/gZYFan)

* <u>Inhalant use disorder</u>

* The features of <u>substance use disorders</u> listed in the “Overview” section are applicable to <u>inhalant use disorder</u>

* Glue sniffer's <u>rash</u>: characteristic <u>eczematous</u> <u>rash</u> between the nose and upper lip after prolonged use of inhalants

* Clinical features of inhalant intoxication [[2]](/library/Nta-dm)[[37]](/library/gZYFan)

* Short duration of symptoms (rapid onset and resolution)

* Lingering odor of inhalant substance

* Slurred speech, <u>headache</u>, <u>diplopia</u>, <u>agitation</u>, <u>hallucinations</u>, gait disturbance, <u>somnolence</u>

* Euphoria, disinhibition, <u>dizziness</u>, confusion, <u>lethargy</u>, <u>disorientation</u>, drowsiness

* <u>Nausea and vomiting</u>

* <u>Nystagmus</u>, <u>muscle weakness</u>, <u>tremor</u>, <u>hyporeflexia</u>, <u>ataxia</u>

* Overdose: <u>asphyxia</u>, suffocation, <u>seizure</u>, <u>coma</u>, <u>death</u> (due to respiratory <u>depression</u>)

* Clinical features of withdrawal: usually no <u>withdrawal symptoms</u>, but regular users may develop symptoms of <u>CNS</u> excitation (e.g., <u>tachycardia</u>, irritability, <u>hallucinations</u>, <u>dysphoria</u>, <u>insomnia</u>, <u>headache</u>)

* Treatment [[37]](/library/gZYFan)

* Supportive treatment, reassurance

* <u>Intubation</u> may be necessary

* <u>Psychotherapy</u>

* Complications [[37]](/library/gZYFan)

* Impaired <u>cognition</u>

* <u>Peripheral neuropathy</u>

* <u>Malignancy</u>

* <u>Aplastic anemia</u>

* <u>Myocarditis</u> and <u>myocardial infarction</u>

* <u>Urinary calculi</u>

* <u>Glomerulonephritis</u>

---

## Opioid-related disorders

See “<u>Opioid use disorder</u>“ for details.




* Substance: <u>opiates</u> (<u>fentanyl</u>, <u>oxycodone</u>, <u>hydrocodone</u>; heroin)

* Street names

* Smack and dope (<u>heroin</u>)

* The blues, fenty powder (<u>fentanyl</u>)

* Forms of preparation: illegal or prescription drugs for oral ingestion, injection, smoking, snorting

* Mechanism of action

* κ-, δ-, and <u>μ-receptor</u> <u>agonists</u> (<u>morphine</u>, <u>heroin</u>, <u>codeine</u>, <u>fentanyl</u>)

* Mixed <u>agonist</u>/<u>antagonist</u> action (<u>buprenorphine</u>)

---

## Sedative, hypnotic, and anxiolytic related disorders

See <u>benzodiazepine overdose</u>, <u>benzodiazepine dependence</u>, and <u>barbiturate intoxication</u> in the article on <u>sedative-hypnotic drug overdose</u>.

---

## Stimulant-related disorders

See “<u>Stimulant intoxication and withdrawal</u>” for evaluation and management of acute intoxication and withdrawal of stimulant drugs.




* Definition: <u>Stimulant-related disorders</u> encompass conditions caused by <u>cocaine</u>, <u>amphetamines</u>, <u>amphetamine</u>-substituted substances, and <u>synthetic cathinones</u>.

* Examples

* Cocaine use disorder

* Amphetamine use disorder

* Diagnostic criteria: Use the <u>DSM-V</u> criteria for general <u>substance use disorders</u>.

* Treatment

* <u>Cocaine use disorder</u>: <u>psychotherapy</u>, group programs  [[38]](/library/SJWytm0)

* <u>Amphetamine</u> and <u>methamphetamine</u> use disorder: <u>psychotherapy</u> and support programs  [[39]](/library/lQWvwO0)

* <u>Synthetic cathinone</u> dependence: <u>psychotherapy</u> and support programs

---

## Tobacco-related disorders

See “<u>Tobacco product use and smoking cessation</u>.”

---

## Gambling disorder

<u>Gambling disorder</u> is a non-substance-related addictive disorder characterized by persistent and recurrent <u>gambling</u> that results in functional impairment.  [[1]](/library/muWV7M0)




### <u>Epidemiology</u> [[1]](/library/muWV7M0)




* <u>♂</u> > <u>♀</u>

* More prevalent in younger and middle-aged individuals





### Etiology [[1]](/library/muWV7M0)




* Combination of factors (genetic, environmental, neurochemical abnormalities)

* Often occurs in conjunction with other psychiatric disorders (e.g., <u>antisocial personality disorder</u>, <u>depressive disorder</u>, <u>bipolar disorder</u>, <u>substance use disorders</u>)





### Diagnosis [[1]](/library/muWV7M0)[[40]](/library/s-dtAs0)[[41]](/library/G-dBAs0)




* Perform <u>suicide risk screening</u>.  [[1]](/library/muWV7M0)[[40]](/library/s-dtAs0)

* Consider using a screening tool to help identify patients with <u>gambling disorder</u>.

* Diagnosis is based on the <u>DSM-5</u> criteria.





#### DSM-5 diagnostic criteria for gambling disorder [[1]](/library/muWV7M0)




* ≥ 4 of the following criteria are present in a 12-month period, and behavior is not due to a <u>manic episode</u>:

* Using increasing amounts of money to gamble

* Restlessness or irritability when attempting to stop <u>gambling</u>

* Multiple failed attempts to quit <u>gambling</u>

* Frequent preoccupation with <u>gambling</u>

* <u>Gambling</u> when feeling helpless, guilty, anxious, or depressed

* Repeated <u>gambling</u> in an attempt to undo losses (“chasing one's losses”)

* Lying to conceal the extent of <u>gambling</u>

* Relying on others for financial support to maintain habit

* Jeopardizing relationships or career as a result of <u>gambling</u>

* Severity is based on the number of criteria met.

* Mild: 4–5

* Moderate: 6–7

* Severe: 8–9





### Treatment [[40]](/library/s-dtAs0)[[41]](/library/G-dBAs0)




* Treat comorbidities, e.g.:   [[1]](/library/muWV7M0)[[40]](/library/s-dtAs0)[[41]](/library/G-dBAs0)

* <u>Treatment of alcohol use disorder</u> (e.g., with <u>naltrexone</u>)

* <u>Treatment of bipolar disorder</u> (e.g., with <u>lithium</u>)

* <u>Treatment of depression</u> (e.g., with an <u>SSRI</u>)

* Refer for psychosocial interventions, e.g.: [[42]](/library/ebVxsG0)[[43]](/library/hbVctG0)

* <u>Motivational interviewing</u>

* <u>Cognitive behavioral therapy</u>

* Provide information on community resources, e.g.:

* <u>Gamblers Anonymous</u>  [[40]](/library/s-dtAs0)

* National Problem <u>Gambling</u> Helpline to provide support and information on support services

* In consultation with a <u>psychiatrist</u>, consider <u>off-label use</u> of an <u>opioid</u> <u>receptor</u> <u>antagonist</u> (e.g., <u>naltrexone</u>).  [[44]](/library/nZV7XG0)[[45]](/library/MZVMXG0)





> [!TIP]
> Offer a combination of interventions to increase the likelihood of recovery. [[40]](/library/s-dtAs0)[[41]](/library/G-dBAs0)




#### Patients not currently interested in treatment




* Offer treatment for psychiatric comorbidities.

* Consider a <u>brief intervention for gambling</u>. [[40]](/library/s-dtAs0)[[46]](/library/icVJXt0)

* Advise patients they can return at any point to start treatment.





### Complications [[1]](/library/muWV7M0)




* <u>Suicidal ideation</u> and behavior [[40]](/library/s-dtAs0)

* Associated with poor general health, including <u>tachycardia</u> and <u>angina</u> [[1]](/library/muWV7M0)

---

## Gamma-hydroxybutyric acid use

### Pharmacology




* Substances (street names: G, Georgia home boy, <u>liquid ecstasy</u>, liquid X) [[47]](/library/IqWY-m0)[[48]](/library/rqWf-m0)

* <u>GHB</u>: <u>recreational drug</u> used to induce euphoria, disinhibition, enhanced empathy, and/or increased libido  [[48]](/library/rqWf-m0)

* <u>GHB</u> is also used as a <u>performance-enhancing drug</u> by athletes.  [[49]](/library/J1ds3K0)

* Mechanism of action: direct <u>agonist</u> of <u>GABA</u> <u>receptors</u> (similar to <u>benzodiazepines</u>) [[50]](/library/bKbHUu)

* <u>Pharmacokinetics</u> [[47]](/library/IqWY-m0)[[48]](/library/rqWf-m0)

* Onset: 15–20 minutes

* Peak effect: 30–60 minutes

* <u>Half-life</u>: 20–50 minutes (dose-dependent)





> [!TIP]
> <u>GHB</u> is sometimes used in <u>drug-facilitated sexual assault</u> because of its rapid onset, amnesic effect, and difficult detection. [[47]](/library/IqWY-m0)[[48]](/library/rqWf-m0)




### Risky substance use




* Acute intoxication: See “<u>GHB intoxication and overdose</u>.”

* Chronic <u>GHB</u> use and dependence [[51]](/library/WddPKK0)

* Most common in young men

* Tolerance can cause dose escalation, which increases the risk of <u>GHB overdose</u>.

* <u>Withdrawal symptoms</u> can lead to frequent reuse (e.g., every few hours).





### GHB withdrawal [[47]](/library/IqWY-m0)[[52]](/library/qqWCzm0)




Abrupt cessation of chronic <u>GHB</u> use can precipitate a potentially fatal withdrawal syndrome.




#### Clinical features [[47]](/library/IqWY-m0)[[52]](/library/qqWCzm0)




The clinical features of <u>GHB withdrawal</u> are similar to those of <u>alcohol withdrawal</u> and <u>benzodiazepine withdrawal</u>. [[47]](/library/IqWY-m0)




* <u>CNS</u> stimulation: <u>tremor</u>, increased muscle tone, <u>seizures</u>, <u>coma</u>

* Neuropsychiatric changes

* <u>Insomnia</u>, irritability, <u>anxiety</u>, <u>agitation</u>, <u>psychosis</u>

* Confusion, <u>delirium</u>, <u>hallucinations</u>

* Autonomic stimulation: <u>tachycardia</u>, <u>hypertension</u>, <u>diaphoresis</u>

* GI: <u>nausea</u>, <u>vomiting</u>, abdominal cramping, <u>diarrhea</u>





> [!TIP]
> Features of <u>GHB withdrawal</u> may appear as early as 1–6 hours after the last ingestion and persist for over 14 days. [[47]](/library/IqWY-m0)




#### Management [[47]](/library/IqWY-m0)[[52]](/library/qqWCzm0)




* Begin high-dose <u>benzodiazepine</u> therapy (e.g., <u>diazepam</u>, <u>lorazepam</u>).

* Urgently consult <u>psychiatry</u> or addiction medicine to guide pharmacotherapy.  [[47]](/library/IqWY-m0)[[53]](/library/AN1Rdh0)

* Consider admission to the <u>ICU</u> for severe symptoms or if high doses of sedatives are required.

* Monitor for complications including <u>seizures</u>, <u>rhabdomyolysis</u>, and <u>hyperthermia</u>.





> [!WARNING]
> Acute <u>GHB withdrawal</u> is a <u>medical emergency</u> and may result in <u>death</u> if not appropriately diagnosed and managed. [[47]](/library/IqWY-m0)[[52]](/library/qqWCzm0)
